basis: Bothy's own wording, following published first-aid guidance: Resuscitation Council UK and European Resuscitation Council guidelines (2021), NHS, British Red Cross and St John Ambulance.
disclaimer: First aid only, not a substitute for training or a doctor. If you can, call the emergency number first. These cards have not yet been checked by a medical professional.
call: Call the emergency number: 112 works from most mobile phones (also 999 in the UK, 911 in North America, 000 in Australia).
match: A query shows a card if it contains one of its keywords, or one of its weak words together with one of its with words (a different word); never if it contains one of its not words. Words and phrases match whole words, case-insensitive, apostrophes removed (wont, isnt).

cards.title: Not breathing: CPR
cards.when: They don't respond and aren't breathing normally (gasping is not normal breathing).
steps: Make sure it is safe. Shout to them and gently shake their shoulders.
No response: tilt the head back, lift the chin, and look, listen and feel for normal breathing for up to 10 seconds.
Not breathing normally: call the emergency number and put the phone on speaker. Send someone for a defibrillator (AED) if there is one nearby.
Kneel beside them. Put the heel of one hand in the centre of the chest, the other hand on top, arms straight.
Push down hard, 5 to 6 cm, then let the chest come back up. Go fast: 100 to 120 pushes a minute, about 2 a second.

If you are trained and willing, give 2 rescue breaths after every 30 pushes: tilt the head, pinch the nose, seal your mouth over theirs and blow for 1 second until the chest rises. Otherwise just keep pushing.
When the AED arrives, switch it on and do what it says.
Don't stop until help takes over, they start breathing normally, or you are too exhausted to go on. Swap with someone every 2 minutes if you can.
children: Child (1 year to puberty): give 5 rescue breaths first, then 30 pushes to 2 breaths. Push one third of the chest depth (about 5 cm) with one or two hands.

Baby (under 1 year): head level, not tipped back. Cover the mouth and nose with your mouth and give 5 gentle breaths, then 30 pushes with two fingers in the centre of the chest (about 4 cm), then 2 breaths, and repeat.
Call on speaker straight away if you can. If you have to leave to get help, give CPR for about 1 minute first.
Drowning: give 5 rescue breaths first, then CPR.
dont: Don't stop to check again unless they wake up, move, open their eyes or breathe normally.

cards.title: Choking
cards.when: They can't speak, breathe or cough, and may clutch at their throat.
steps: If they can cough, tell them to keep coughing.
If coughing doesn't clear it: lean them forward, support their chest with one hand, and give up to 5 sharp blows between the shoulder blades with the heel of your other hand. Check after each one.
Still choking: stand behind them, put your fist just above the belly button, grab it with your other hand and pull sharply in and up. Up to 5 times.
Repeat 5 back blows and 5 abdominal thrusts. If it hasn't cleared, call the emergency number and keep going.
If they become unresponsive, call the emergency number and start CPR.
Anyone who has had abdominal thrusts should see a doctor afterwards.
children: Child over 1: as for adults; kneel or sit behind a small child.
Baby under 1: lay the baby face down along your thigh, head lower than the bottom, supporting the head. Give up to 5 back blows.
Still choking: turn the baby face up on your thigh and give up to 5 chest thrusts with two fingers in the centre of the chest.
Never give abdominal thrusts to a baby. Keep repeating, and call the emergency number if it doesn't clear.
dont: Don't feel blindly in the mouth: you can push the object further in. Only remove it if you can see it and pick it out easily.
cards.call_if: The blockage doesn't clear, they become unresponsive, or abdominal thrusts were used.

cards.title: Severe bleeding
cards.when: Blood is spurting, pouring or soaking through clothes.
steps: Call the emergency number, or get someone else to. Protect your hands with gloves or a plastic bag if you can.
Press hard on the wound with a clean pad or cloth, or your hand. Keep pressing for at least 10 minutes without lifting to look.
If blood soaks through, put another pad on top and keep pressing. Don't take the first one off.
When the bleeding slows, bandage the pad firmly in place. Check that the fingers or toes beyond it stay warm and pink.

Life-threatening bleeding from an arm or leg that pressure can't stop: put a tourniquet (or a wide strap twisted tight with a stick) 5 to 7 cm above the wound, not on a joint. Tighten until the bleeding stops and note the time. Don't loosen it.
If something is stuck in the wound, leave it in and press on either side of it.
Lay them down and keep them warm (see Shock).
dont: Don't pull out anything stuck in the wound.
Don't use thin string or wire as a tourniquet.
cards.call_if: Bleeding is heavy, won't stop, or comes from a deep or large wound.

cards.title: Shock
cards.when: After an injury, bleeding, burns or severe illness: pale, cold, clammy skin; fast weak pulse; fast breathing; dizzy, confused or drowsy.
steps: Call the emergency number.
Treat the cause if you can, such as bleeding.
Lay them down. Raise their legs and support them, unless a leg is injured.
Keep them warm with a coat or blanket, under and over them if they are on cold ground.
Loosen tight clothing and reassure them.
Keep checking their breathing. If it stops, start CPR.
dont: Don't give them anything to eat or drink.
Don't leave them alone.

cards.title: Burns and scalds
cards.when: Skin burnt by heat, hot liquid, chemicals, electricity or the sun.
steps: Stop the burning: move away from the heat. Clothes on fire: stop, drop and roll. Electricity: switch it off before you touch them.
Cool the burn under cool or lukewarm running water for 20 minutes. Start as soon as you can.
Take off clothing and jewellery near the burn, unless it is stuck to the skin.
Keep the rest of them warm while you cool the burn, especially a child.
After cooling, cover loosely with cling film laid on lengthways (not wrapped round) or a clean plastic bag.
Chemical burn: brush off any dry chemical, then rinse with plenty of running water for at least 20 minutes.
Paracetamol or ibuprofen can help the pain (follow the packet).
dont: No ice, iced water, butter, creams, oils or toothpaste.
Don't burst blisters or peel off stuck clothing.
Don't use fluffy dressings or cotton wool.
cards.call_if: The burn is bigger than the person's hand; on the face, hands, feet, joints or genitals; deep (white, brown or charred); from chemicals or electricity; they breathed in smoke; or they are a child, elderly or pregnant.

cards.title: Stroke: FAST
cards.when: Sudden weakness, numbness or confusion, often on one side of the body.
steps: Face: has their face drooped on one side? Can they smile?
Arms: can they lift both arms and keep them up?
Speech: is their speech slurred, or are they confused?
Time: call the emergency number straight away if you see any one of these.
Note the time the symptoms started: doctors need it.
Keep them comfortable and reassure them. If they become unresponsive but are breathing, put them in the recovery position.
dont: Don't give them food, drink or medicine, including aspirin.
cards.call_if: Always, even if the symptoms go away.

cards.title: Heart attack
cards.when: Chest pain or pressure (tight, heavy, squeezing) that may spread to the arms, neck, jaw, back or stomach; breathless, sweating, sick or dizzy. It can be mild, especially in women, older people and people with diabetes.
steps: Call the emergency number straight away.
Sit them down, leaning back with knees bent, and keep them calm.
If they are an adult and not allergic to it, give one 300 mg aspirin to chew slowly.
If they have their own medicine for angina (such as a spray under the tongue), help them take it.
Loosen tight clothing and stay with them.
If they become unresponsive and stop breathing normally, start CPR and send for a defibrillator (AED).
dont: Don't let them walk about or exert themselves.
Don't give aspirin to children under 16 or anyone allergic to it.

cards.title: Poisoning
cards.when: They have swallowed, breathed in or touched something harmful: bleach, cleaners, medicines, alcohol, plants, mushrooms, chemicals, antifreeze.
steps: Call the emergency number or a poison centre now, even if they seem fine. Some poisons, like a paracetamol overdose, only cause harm hours later.
Find out what it was, how much and when. Keep the container, packet or plant to show.
Bleach or another corrosive swallowed: rinse the mouth with water and spit it out. If they are awake and can swallow, small sips of water or milk while you get advice.
On the skin or in the eyes: rinse with plenty of running water for 20 minutes, and take off contaminated clothing.
Fumes: get them into fresh air without putting yourself at risk.
Unresponsive but breathing: recovery position. Not breathing: CPR (if the poison is on their lips, do chest pushes only).
Swallowed a button battery or magnets: go to hospital at once, even with no symptoms.
dont: Don't make them sick: no fingers down the throat, no salt water.
Don't give anything else to eat or drink unless the poison centre or a doctor tells you to.

cards.title: Unresponsive but breathing
cards.when: They don't respond but are breathing normally: put them in the recovery position so they can't choke.
steps: Call the emergency number.
Kneel beside them. Put the arm nearest you at a right angle to their body, palm up.
Bring their far arm across their chest and hold the back of that hand against their near cheek.
With your other hand, pull their far knee up so the foot is flat on the ground.
Pull on the knee to roll them towards you onto their side.
Tilt the head back and lift the chin so they can breathe easily. Bend the top leg so hip and knee are at right angles.
Keep checking their breathing until help comes. If it stops, start CPR.
children: Baby: hold them in your arms, face down, head lower than the body, supporting the head.
dont: If you think they hurt their neck or back, only move them if you must, keeping head, neck and body in line.

cards.title: Hypothermia (too cold)
cards.when: Shivering, cold pale skin, slurred speech, confusion, clumsiness, drowsiness. When shivering stops, it is getting severe.
steps: Get them out of the cold, wet and wind: indoors or into shelter, and off the cold ground.
Take off wet clothes and put on dry layers. Cover the head.
Warm them gradually: blankets, a sleeping bag, or skin-to-skin contact with another person under the covers.
Warm (not hot) packs or bottles wrapped in cloth can go on the armpits, chest and groin.
If they are fully awake and can swallow, give warm sweet drinks and high-energy food.
Handle them gently. If they are drowsy or confused, keep them lying down.
If they stop breathing normally, start CPR.
dont: Don't rub or massage their arms and legs.
No alcohol, no hot bath or shower, and no direct heat such as a fire or hot water bottle on the skin.
No drinks if they are drowsy or can't swallow properly.
cards.call_if: They are confused, drowsy, unresponsive, have stopped shivering, or are a baby or elderly.

cards.title: Heat exhaustion and heatstroke
cards.when: In heat or after exertion: headache, dizziness, heavy sweating, cramps, feeling sick, fast pulse. Heatstroke is worse: hot skin, confusion, fits or collapse, and they may stop sweating.
steps: Move them to a cool, shady place. Lie them down and raise their feet a little.
If they are awake, give plenty of water, or a rehydration or sports drink.
Cool the skin: spray or sponge with cool water and fan them. Cold packs wrapped in cloth on the armpits and neck help.
They should feel better within 30 minutes.
Heatstroke (confused, fitting, collapsed, or hot and not sweating): call the emergency number and cool them fast, ideally in cool water up to the neck, or by soaking and fanning the whole body.
Unresponsive but breathing: recovery position.
dont: Don't give drinks to someone who is confused or drowsy.
cards.call_if: They don't improve within 30 minutes, are confused, have a fit, collapse, or have hot dry skin.

cards.title: Seizure (fit)
cards.when: Sudden jerking or stiffening, collapse, loss of awareness.
steps: Stay with them and note the time it started.
Protect them: move hard or sharp things away and cushion their head.
Loosen anything tight around the neck.
When the jerking stops, put them in the recovery position and check their breathing.
Stay with them, calm and reassuring, until they are fully awake.
dont: Don't hold them down or try to stop the movements.
Don't put anything in their mouth.
Don't give food or drink until they are fully awake.
cards.call_if: It's their first seizure, it lasts more than 5 minutes, another follows, they are injured, have trouble breathing, don't wake up, or it happened in water.

cards.title: Severe allergic reaction
cards.when: Swelling of the lips, tongue or throat; trouble breathing or swallowing; wheezing; hoarse voice; feeling faint; often after a food, sting or medicine.
steps: Use their adrenaline auto-injector (such as an EpiPen) straight away: into the outer thigh, through clothing if needed.
Call the emergency number and say "anaphylaxis".
Lie them down with their legs raised. If breathing is hard, let them sit up instead.
If they are no better after 5 minutes, give a second auto-injector if there is one.
If they stop breathing normally, start CPR.
dont: Don't let them stand up or walk, even if they feel better.
cards.call_if: Always, even if the injector has worked.

cards.title: Asthma attack
cards.when: Wheezing, coughing, tight chest, too breathless to speak or eat.
steps: Help them sit up straight and stay calm. Loosen tight clothing.
One puff of their reliever inhaler (usually blue) every 30 to 60 seconds, up to 10 puffs. A spacer helps if they have one.
If they feel worse, or are no better after 10 puffs, call the emergency number.
If help takes more than 15 minutes, give up to 10 more puffs the same way.
dont: Don't make them lie down.
cards.call_if: No better after 10 puffs, getting worse, too breathless to speak, lips turning blue, or very tired.

cards.title: Low blood sugar (diabetes)
cards.when: Someone with diabetes is shaky, sweaty, pale, hungry, confused or irritable.
steps: If they are awake and can swallow: give fast sugar, such as a glass of fruit juice or a non-diet fizzy drink, 4 to 5 glucose tablets, or a handful of sweets.
Check again after 10 to 15 minutes. If they are no better, give fast sugar again.
Once they feel better, give some starchy food, such as a sandwich or biscuits.
Unresponsive: put them in the recovery position and call the emergency number.
dont: Don't give food or drink to someone who is drowsy or can't swallow.
cards.call_if: They are unresponsive, have a fit, or don't improve after two lots of sugar.
